title: Elastic drain amplification and variant-escape postmortem
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Summary: On 2026-03-09 17:12 UTC an anomalous decommission signal originated from the eu-west-1 region controller and was interpreted by the routing plane as a hard drain for ~22s. The routing decision engine responded by aggressively shifting traffic away from eu-west-1 and concurrently failing over to cheaper fallback variants in other regions. This produced a rapid fanout of variant fallbacks, a regional cold-start wave, amplified latencies, and a 3x spike in token cost for affected customers.

Timeline highlights: 
- 17:12:04 UTC: controller emitted decommission signal due to an overloaded maintenance job (long-running container GC). Signal incorrectly marked as priority=hard instead of soft.
- 17:12:07 UTC: control plane routing delta computed; several proximity and tier scoring heuristics treated the signal as immediate drain and started rerouting.
- 17:12:08-17:12:30 UTC: automatic fallback policy triggered variant-escape rules (fallback to low-memory quantized variants) to sustain throughput, causing wider cache misses and KV cold starts.
- 17:12:30-17:20:00 UTC: transient tail latencies increased, error budget burn; traffic churn stabilized after kill-switch threshold was reached and automated rollback to original variants completed.

Root cause: 
1) Controller bug: a maintenance GC job overloaded the controller and returned an incorrectly escalated drain signal (priority header inversion).
2) Routing policy sensitivity: the scoring function assigned excessive weight to the drain signal in the presence of concurrent slot-count volatility, producing an all-or-nothing routing delta.
3) Fallback chaining: the fallback rules allowed immediate cross-region variant substitution without a staged canary, which amplified cold-start/quantization side-effects across regions.

Immediate mitigations applied: 
- Emergency hotfix to controller that ensures priority header is validated and capped before emitting drain signals (PR #4782).
- Deployed a temporary dampening window (15s) in the routing delta processor to prevent sub-30s hard reassignments.
- Rolled back aggressive fallback thresholds to require a 2-step canary substitution for cross-region variant changes.

Longer-term fixes and design changes: 
- Routing policy hardening (ENG-60200): refactor scoring to include signal confidence, slot-stability heuristic, and a maximum per-cycle reassign quota.
- Fallback orchestration (ENG-60410): introduce staged fallback flows that prefer intra-region soft-variants and enforce KV-prefill for quantized variants before accepting traffic.
- Controller resiliency (ENG-60650): circuit-break the maintenance GC job and add observability to prevent CPU-saturation-induced mis-signaling.

What went well: 
- Automated rollback thresholds triggered and limited total downtime to <10 minutes for the majority of requests.
- Alerting routed to on-call SREs within 90s and the incident commander coordinated cross-team mitigations quickly.

Follow-ups and owners (action items): 
- ENG-60200 (Marco Nguyen): implement scoring refactor and add unit tests for priority inversion scenarios. Target: 2026-03-28.
- ENG-60410 (Priya Shah): implement staged fallback orchestration and KV-prefill mechanism. Target: 2026-04-04.
- ENG-60650 (Liam O'Connor): controller GC circuit-breaker + metrics. Target: 2026-03-21.
- Docs (Marco Nguyen): update routing runbook to include drain-confidence checks and cross-region fallback playbook. Due: 2026-03-18.

Lessons learned: 
- Single numeric signals (drain=true) are brittle; introduce richer signal metadata (confidence, source, TTL).
- Immediate cross-region substitutions are high-risk when variants differ in memory/quantization profile. Prefill and canary are necessary.
- Observability gaps: need token-level tracing that correlates variant swaps with KV cache miss rates for faster RCA.
